At [[Metacritic]], which assigns a [[Standard score|normalized]] rating out of 100 to reviews from mainstream publications, ''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' received an [[Weighted arithmetic mean|average]] score of 73, indicating "generally favorable reviews".<ref name="MC" /> Critics generally praised the EP's sound; [[AllMusic]] described it as one of the most innovative releases of the 2000s [[Garage rock|garage rock revival]] at the time,<ref name="AllMusic" /> while [[Everett True]] wrote that it captured the spirit of rock n' roll.<ref name=":9" /> Karen O's performances were highlighted for additional praise, with writers for [[Blender (magazine)|''Blender'']] and ''[[CMJ]]'' describing her as "hot and sexy".<ref name=":11">{{cite magazine |last=Santangelo |first=Antonia |date=July 8, 2002 |title=Reviews |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aBw3t2fY64UC&pg=PA10-IA2 |magazine=CMJ New Music Report |page=12 |volume=72 |issue=770 |issn=0890-0795}}</ref><ref name="Blender" /> Some criticism was directed at its [[sound quality]], which was seen as limiting its potential,<ref name="RS" /> while a [[Stylus Magazine|''Stylus'']] writer found three of its five tracks unremarkable.<ref name="Stylus" /> [[Pitchfork (website)|''Pitchfork'']] noted early skepticism surrounding the rock movement but concluded that the EP demonstrated a "sharp survey" of the band's capabilities.<ref name="Pitchfork" />   

In 2002, ''[[NME]]'' ranked ''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' second on its list of the year's best singles.<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 10, 2016 |title=NME's best albums and tracks of 2002 |url=https://www.nme.com/features/2002-2-1045353 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250124234412/https://www.nme.com/features/2002-2-1045353 |archive-date=January 24, 2025 |access-date=February 12, 2026 |website=[[NME]]}}</ref> In the 2004 edition of ''[[The Rolling Stone Album Guide]]'', [[Sasha Frere-Jones]] awarded the EP four stars, writing that the band "instantly made their case for good-old-fashioned attitude"; the EP scored higher than their acclaimed debut album, ''[[Fever to Tell]]''.<ref name="RSAG" /> In 2016, ''[[Under the Radar (magazine)|Under the Radar]]'' ranked it among the best albums of its year, and said that it was essential both to the band's success and the contemporary [[Music of New York City|New York music scene]].<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Berlyant |first=Matthew |date=December 29, 2016 |title=The 15th anniversary: Yeah Yeah Yeahs' "Yeah Yeah Yeahs" EP |url=https://www.undertheradarmag.com/news/the_15th_anniversary_yeah_yeah_yeahs_yeah_yeah_yeahs_ep/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240221192539/https://www.undertheradarmag.com/news/the_15th_anniversary_yeah_yeah_yeahs_yeah_yeah_yeahs_ep/ |archive-date=February 21, 2024 |access-date=March 24, 2026 |magazine=[[Under the Radar (magazine)|Under the Radar]]}}</ref> In 2024, writers for ''[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]'' ranked it at number 42 on their list of the "100 Greatest EPs of All Time", writing that it built on the early works of contemporaries like [[the Strokes]] and [[Interpol (band)|Interpol]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=September 25, 2024 |title=The 100 Greatest EPs of All Time |url=https://www.pastemagazine.com/music/greatest-albums/the-100-greatest-eps-of-all-time |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260130195229/https://www.pastemagazine.com/music/greatest-albums/the-100-greatest-eps-of-all-time |archive-date=January 30, 2026 |access-date=March 6, 2026 |website=[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]}}</ref>

'''''Yeah Yeah Yeahs''''' (often mistitled as '''''Master''''') is the debut [[extended play]] (EP) by the American indie rock band [[Yeah Yeah Yeahs]]. After forming in 2000 and building a reputation with their live shows, Yeah Yeah Yeahs recorded and produced the EP with Jerry Teel, a member of [[Boss Hog]]. It is a record featuring the band's early [[garage rock]] and [[art punk]] influences. It was [[self-released]] on July 9, 2001, and reissued in April 2002 by [[Touch and Go Records|Touch and Go]] and [[Wichita Recordings|Wichita]] in the United States and United Kingdom, respectively.  

''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' was received positively by critics and ranked by ''[[NME]]'' as the second best single of 2002. It received little attention upon release but became a [[sleeper hit]] after its reissue, topping the [[UK Independent Singles and Albums Charts|UK Indie Chart]] and exceeding sales of 71,000 units in the United States by the end of the decade. In 2024, [[Paste (magazine)|''Paste'']] ranked it among the greatest EPs ever made.

By late 2001, Yeah Yeah Yeahs gained a following for their live shows.<ref name="RS" /><ref name="timesonline20092">{{cite web |last=McLean |first=Craig |date=June 13, 2009 |title=Yeah Yeah Yeahs: why fans of the art-punk trio can't say no |url=http://entertainment.timesonline.co.uk/tol/arts_and_entertainment/music/article6485717.ece |url-status= |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110615161512/http://entertainment.timesonline.co.uk/tol/arts_and_entertainment/music/article6485717.ece |archive-date=June 15, 2011 |access-date=March 13, 2026 |work=[[The Times]]}}</ref> Around this time, they enlisted Jerry Teel, a former guitarist for the punk rock band [[Boss Hog]], to co-produce their debut [[Extended play|EP]].<ref name=":1" /> They recorded it at the short-lived Funhouse Recording Studio with Teel, while Chuck Scott [[Mastering (audio)|mastered]] it at Soundoptik in New York City. Its art and packaging were designed by the band and Crispin.<ref name=":0" /> Although it is self-titled, the EP is sometimes incorrectly referred to as ''Master'' due to the necklace Karen O wears on the cover.<ref name=":1" />

''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' is an [[alternative rock]], [[art punk]], [[garage rock]], and [[indie rock]] EP.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":8">{{Cite web |last=Clarke |first=Betty |date=April 26, 2009 |title=Yeah Yeah Yeahs |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2009/apr/27/yeah-yeahs-pop-review |access-date=March 13, 2026 |website=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> It consists of five tracks and runs for 13 minutes and 52 seconds.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" /> The songs were written by Karen O, whose [[staccato]] vocals became a focal point of the record,<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |last=True |first=Everett |author-link=Everett True |date=2002 |title=Another ancient interview with Yeah Yeah Yeahs. The opening track, "Bang", is about Karen O's sexual dissatisfaction with an ex-boyfriend,<ref>{{Cite web |last=True |first=Everett |author-link=Everett True |date=August 2002 |title=An ancient interview with Yeah Yeah Yeahs. At [[Metacritic]], which assigns a [[Standard score|normalized]] rating out of 100 to reviews from mainstream publications, ''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' received an [[Weighted arithmetic mean|average]] score of 73, indicating "generally favorable reviews".<ref name="MC" /> Critics generally praised the EP's sound; [[AllMusic]] described it as one of the most innovative releases of the 2000s [[Garage rock|garage rock revival]] at the time,<ref name="AllMusic" /> while [[Everett True]] wrote that it captured the spirit of rock n' roll.<ref name=":9" /> Karen O's performances were highlighted for additional praise, with writers for [[Blender (magazine)|''Blender'']] and ''[[CMJ]]'' describing her as "hot and sexy".<ref name=":11">{{cite magazine |last=Santangelo |first=Antonia |date=July 8, 2002 |title=Reviews |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aBw3t2fY64UC&pg=PA10-IA2 |magazine=CMJ New Music Report |page=12 |volume=72 |issue=770 |issn=0890-0795}}</ref><ref name="Blender" /> Some criticism was directed at its [[sound quality]], which was seen as limiting its potential,<ref name="RS" /> while a [[Stylus Magazine|''Stylus'']] writer found three of its five tracks unremarkable.<ref name="Stylus" /> [[Pitchfork (website)|''Pitchfork'']] noted early skepticism surrounding the rock movement but concluded that the EP demonstrated a "sharp survey" of the band's capabilities.<ref name="Pitchfork" />

the EP scored higher than their acclaimed debut album, ''[[Fever to Tell]]''.<ref name="RSAG" /> In 2016, ''[[Under the Radar (magazine)|Under the Radar]]'' ranked it among the best albums of its year, and said that it was essential both to the band's success and the contemporary [[Music of New York City|New York music scene]].<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Berlyant |first=Matthew |date=December 29, 2016 |title=The 15th anniversary: Yeah Yeah Yeahs' "Yeah Yeah Yeahs" EP |url=https://www.undertheradarmag.com/news/the_15th_anniversary_yeah_yeah_yeahs_yeah_yeah_yeahs_ep/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240221192539/https://www.undertheradarmag.com/news/the_15th_anniversary_yeah_yeah_yeahs_yeah_yeah_yeahs_ep/ |archive-date=February 21, 2024 |access-date=March 24, 2026 |magazine=[[Under the Radar (magazine)|Under the Radar]]}}</ref> In 2024, writers for ''[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]'' ranked it at number 42 on their list of the "100 Greatest EPs of All Time", writing that it built on the early works of contemporaries like [[the Strokes]] and [[Interpol (band)|Interpol]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=September 25, 2024 |title=The 100 Greatest EPs of All Time |url=https://www.pastemagazine.com/music/greatest-albums/the-100-greatest-eps-of-all-time |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260130195229/https://www.pastemagazine.com/music/greatest-albums/the-100-greatest-eps-of-all-time |archive-date=January 30, 2026 |access-date=March 6, 2026 |website=[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]}}</ref>

'''''Yeah Yeah Yeahs''''' (often mistitled as '''''Master''''') is the debut [[extended play]] (EP) by the American indie rock band [[Yeah Yeah Yeahs]]. After forming in 2000 and building a reputation with their live shows, Yeah Yeah Yeahs recorded and produced the EP with Jerry Teel, a member of [[Boss Hog]]. It is a record featuring the band's early [[garage rock]] and [[art punk]] influences. It was [[self-released]] on July 9, 2001, and reissued in April 2002 by [[Touch and Go Records|Touch and Go]] and [[Wichita Recordings|Wichita]] in the United States and United Kingdom, respectively.  

''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' was received positively by critics and ranked by ''[[NME]]'' as the second best single of 2002. It received little attention upon release but became a [[sleeper hit]] after its reissue, topping the [[UK Independent Singles and Albums Charts|UK Indie Chart]] and exceeding sales of 71,000 units in the United States by the end of the decade. In 2024, [[Paste (magazine)|''Paste'']] ranked it among the greatest EPs ever made.

'''''Yeah Yeah Yeahs''''' (often mistitled as '''''Master''''') is the debut [[extended play]] (EP) by the American indie rock band [[Yeah Yeah Yeahs]]. After forming in 2000 and building a reputation with their live shows, Yeah Yeah Yeahs recorded and produced the EP with Jerry Teel, a member of [[Boss Hog]]. It is a record featuring the band's early [[garage rock]] and [[art punk]] influences. It was [[self-released]] on July 9, 2001, and reissued in April 2002 by [[Touch and Go Records|Touch and Go]] and [[Wichita Recordings|Wichita]] in the United States and United Kingdom, respectively.  

''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' was received positively by critics and ranked by ''[[NME]]'' as the second best single of 2002. It received little attention upon release but became a [[sleeper hit]] after its reissue, topping the [[UK Independent Singles and Albums Charts|UK Indie Chart]] and exceeding sales of 71,000 units in the United States by the end of the decade. In 2024, [[Paste (magazine)|''Paste'']] ranked it among the greatest EPs ever made.

'''''Yeah Yeah Yeahs''''' (often mistitled as '''''Master''''') is the debut [[extended play]] (EP) by the American indie rock band [[Yeah Yeah Yeahs]]. After forming in 2000 and building a reputation with their live shows, Yeah Yeah Yeahs recorded and produced the EP with Jerry Teel, a member of [[Boss Hog]]. It is a record featuring the band's early [[garage rock]] and [[art punk]] influences. It was [[self-released]] on July 9, 2001, and reissued in April 2002 by [[Touch and Go Records|Touch and Go]] and [[Wichita Recordings|Wichita]] in the United States and United Kingdom, respectively.  

''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' was received positively by critics and ranked by ''[[NME]]'' as the second best single of 2002. It received little attention upon release but became a [[sleeper hit]] after its reissue, topping the [[UK Independent Singles and Albums Charts|UK Indie Chart]] and exceeding sales of 71,000 units in the United States by the end of the decade. In 2024, [[Paste (magazine)|''Paste'']] ranked it among the greatest EPs ever made.

'''''Yeah Yeah Yeahs''''' (often mistitled as '''''Master''''') is the debut [[extended play]] (EP) by the American indie rock band [[Yeah Yeah Yeahs]]. After forming in 2000 and building a reputation with their live shows, Yeah Yeah Yeahs recorded and produced the EP with Jerry Teel, a member of [[Boss Hog]]. It is a record featuring the band's early [[garage rock]] and [[art punk]] influences. It was [[self-released]] on July 9, 2001, and reissued in April 2002 by [[Touch and Go Records|Touch and Go]] and [[Wichita Recordings|Wichita]] in the United States and United Kingdom, respectively.  

''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' was received positively by critics and ranked by ''[[NME]]'' as the second best single of 2002. It received little attention upon release but became a [[sleeper hit]] after its reissue, topping the [[UK Independent Singles and Albums Charts|UK Indie Chart]] and exceeding sales of 71,000 units in the United States by the end of the decade. In 2024, [[Paste (magazine)|''Paste'']] ranked it among the greatest EPs ever made.

At [[Metacritic]], which assigns a [[Standard score|normalized]] rating out of 100 to reviews from mainstream publications, ''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' received an [[Weighted arithmetic mean|average]] score of 73, indicating "generally favorable reviews".<ref name="MC" /> Critics generally praised the EP's sound; [[AllMusic]] described it as one of the most innovative releases of the 2000s [[Garage rock|garage rock revival]] at the time,<ref name="AllMusic" /> while [[Everett True]] wrote that it captured the spirit of rock n' roll.<ref name=":9" /> Karen O's performances were highlighted for additional praise, with writers for [[Blender (magazine)|''Blender'']] and ''[[CMJ]]'' describing her as "hot and sexy".<ref name=":11">{{cite magazine |last=Santangelo |first=Antonia |date=July 8, 2002 |title=Reviews |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aBw3t2fY64UC&pg=PA10-IA2 |magazine=CMJ New Music Report |page=12 |volume=72 |issue=770 |issn=0890-0795}}</ref><ref name="Blender" /> Some criticism was directed at its [[sound quality]], which was seen as limiting its potential,<ref name="RS" /> while a [[Stylus Magazine|''Stylus'']] writer found three of its five tracks unremarkable.<ref name="Stylus" /> [[Pitchfork (website)|''Pitchfork'']] noted early skepticism surrounding the rock movement but concluded that the EP demonstrated a "sharp survey" of the band's capabilities.<ref name="Pitchfork" />   

In 2002, ''[[NME]]'' ranked ''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' second on its list of the year's best singles.<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 10, 2016 |title=NME's best albums and tracks of 2002 |url=https://www.nme.com/features/2002-2-1045353 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250124234412/https://www.nme.com/features/2002-2-1045353 |archive-date=January 24, 2025 |access-date=February 12, 2026 |website=[[NME]]}}</ref> In the 2004 edition of ''[[The Rolling Stone Album Guide]]'', [[Sasha Frere-Jones]] awarded the EP four stars, writing that the band "instantly made their case for good-old-fashioned attitude"; '''''Yeah Yeah Yeahs''''' (often mistitled as '''''Master''''') is the debut [[extended play]] (EP) by the American indie rock band [[Yeah Yeah Yeahs]]. After forming in 2000 and building a reputation with their live shows, Yeah Yeah Yeahs recorded and produced the EP with Jerry Teel, a member of [[Boss Hog]]. It is a record featuring the band's early [[garage rock]] and [[art punk]] influences. It was [[self-released]] on July 9, 2001, and reissued in April 2002 by [[Touch and Go Records|Touch and Go]] and [[Wichita Recordings|Wichita]] in the United States and United Kingdom, respectively.  

''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' was received positively by critics and ranked by ''[[NME]]'' as the second best single of 2002. It received little attention upon release but became a [[sleeper hit]] after its reissue, topping the [[UK Independent Singles and Albums Charts|UK Indie Chart]] and exceeding sales of 71,000 units in the United States by the end of the decade. In 2024, [[Paste (magazine)|''Paste'']] ranked it among the greatest EPs ever made.

By late 2001, Yeah Yeah Yeahs had gained a live following.<ref name="RS" /><ref name="timesonline20092">{{cite web |last=McLean |first=Craig |date=June 13, 2009 |title=Yeah Yeah Yeahs: why fans of the art-punk trio can't say no |url=http://entertainment.timesonline.co.uk/tol/arts_and_entertainment/music/article6485717.ece |url-status= |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110615161512/http://entertainment.timesonline.co.uk/tol/arts_and_entertainment/music/article6485717.ece |archive-date=June 15, 2011 |access-date=March 13, 2026 |work=[[The Times]]}}</ref> Around this time, they enlisted Jerry Teel, a former guitarist for the punk rock band [[Boss Hog]], to co-produce their debut [[Extended play|EP]].<ref name=":1" /> They recorded it at the short-lived Funhouse Recording Studio with Teel, while Chuck Scott [[Mastering (audio)|mastered]] it at Soundoptik in New York City. '''''Yeah Yeah Yeahs''''' (often mistitled as '''''Master''''') is the debut [[extended play]] (EP) by the American indie rock band [[Yeah Yeah Yeahs]]. After forming in 2000 and building a reputation with their live shows, Yeah Yeah Yeahs recorded and produced the EP with Jerry Teel, a member of [[Boss Hog]]. It is a record featuring the band's early [[garage rock]] and [[art punk]] influences. It was [[self-released]] on July 9, 2001, and reissued in April 2002 by [[Touch and Go Records|Touch and Go]] and [[Wichita Recordings|Wichita]] in the United States and United Kingdom, respectively.  

''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' was received positively by critics and ranked by ''[[NME]]'' as the second best single of 2002. It received little attention upon release but became a [[sleeper hit]] after its reissue, topping the [[UK Independent Singles and Albums Charts|UK Indie Chart]] and exceeding sales of 71,000 units in the United States by the end of the decade. In 2024, [[Paste (magazine)|''Paste'']] ranked it among the greatest EPs ever made.

By late 2001, Yeah Yeah Yeahs had gained a live following.<ref name="RS" /><ref name="timesonline20092">{{cite web |last=McLean |first=Craig |date=June 13, 2009 |title=Yeah Yeah Yeahs: why fans of the art-punk trio can't say no |url=http://entertainment.timesonline.co.uk/tol/arts_and_entertainment/music/article6485717.ece |url-status= |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110615161512/http://entertainment.timesonline.co.uk/tol/arts_and_entertainment/music/article6485717.ece |archive-date=June 15, 2011 |access-date=March 13, 2026 |work=[[The Times]]}}</ref> Around this time, they enlisted Jerry Teel, a former guitarist for the punk rock band [[Boss Hog]], to co-produce their debut [[Extended play|EP]].<ref name=":1" /> They recorded it at the short-lived Funhouse Recording Studio with Teel, while Chuck Scott [[Mastering (audio)|mastered]] it at Soundoptik in New York City. Its art and packaging were designed by the band and Crispin.<ref name=":0" /> Although it is self-titled, the EP is sometimes incorrectly referred to as ''Master'' due to the necklace Karen O wears on the cover.<ref name=":1" />

'''''Yeah Yeah Yeahs''''' (often mistitled as '''''Master''''') is the debut [[extended play]] (EP) by the American indie rock band [[Yeah Yeah Yeahs]]. After forming in 2000 and building a reputation with their live shows, Yeah Yeah Yeahs recorded and produced the EP with Jerry Teel, a member of [[Boss Hog]]. It is a record featuring the band's early [[garage rock]] and [[art punk]] influences. It was [[self-released]] on July 9, 2001, and reissued in 2002 by [[Touch and Go Records|Touch and Go]] and [[Wichita Recordings|Wichita]] in the United States and United Kingdom, respectively.  

''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' was received positively by critics and ranked by ''[[NME]]'' as the second best single of 2002. It received little attention upon release but became a [[sleeper hit]] after its reissue, topping the [[UK Independent Singles and Albums Charts|UK Indie Chart]] and exceeding sales of 71,000 units in the United States by the end of the decade. In 2024, [[Paste (magazine)|''Paste'']] ranked it among the greatest EPs ever made. 

== Background and recording ==
The singer/songwriter [[Karen O]] and guitarist [[Nick Zinner]] founded the acoustic duo Unitard in 2000. They changed their name that year to Yeah Yeah Yeahs and shifted to a "trashy, punky, [and] grimy" sound inspired by the contemporary Ohio music scene.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web |last=Houghton Fader]]}}</ref> 

By 2001, Yeah Yeah Yeahs earned a live following.<ref name="RS" /><ref name="timesonline20092">{{cite web |last=McLean |first=Craig |date=June 13, 2009 |title=Yeah Yeah Yeahs: why fans of the art-punk trio can't say no |url=http://entertainment.timesonline.co.uk/tol/arts_and_entertainment/music/article6485717.ece |url-status= |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110615161512/http://entertainment.timesonline.co.uk/tol/arts_and_entertainment/music/article6485717.ece |archive-date=June 15, 2011 |access-date=March 13, 2026 |work=[[The Times]]}}</ref> During this period, they began creating music and enlisted Jerry Teel, a former guitarist for the punk rock band [[Boss Hog]], to co-produce a [[Demo (music)|demo]] intended to secure more shows. However, they ultimately developed the demo into their debut EP, a decision that Zinner attributes to their desire to share their music.{{Sfn|Goodman|2017|p=229}} It was recorded at [[Avenue B (Manhattan)|Avenue B]]'s Funhouse Recording Studio with Teel—which doubled as their rehearsal space—while Chuck Scott [[Mastering (audio)|mastered]] it at Soundoptik in New York City.{{Sfn|Goodman|2017|p=229}}<ref name=":0" />

The artwork and packaging for ''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' was designed by the band and Crispin.<ref name=":0" /> The front cover is a [[close-up]] of a topless Karen O, and the back cover features three different [[Selfie|self-photographs]] of her, Zinner and Chase.<ref name=":0" /> Although it is self-titled, the EP is sometimes mistitled as ''Master'' due to the necklace Karen O wears on the cover.<ref name=":1" />

== Music and lyrics ==
''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' consists of five tracks and runs for 13 minutes and 52 seconds.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" /> The songs were written by Karen O and its music was composed by the band.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rogers |first=Jude |author-link=Jude Rogers |date=March 14, 2019 |title='I just wanted to write a love song that stands the test of time': Karen O on her best work |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2019/mar/14/all-i-ever-wanted-to-do-was-write-a-love-song-that-stands-the-test-of-time-karen-o-on-her-best-songs |access-date=March 13, 2026 |website=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> The rock band [[ESG (band)|ESG]] served as a primary influence for the EP, with the band attempting to recreate their sound "with guitar instead of bass."<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 29, 2014 |title=Karen O: soundtrack of my life |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2014/aug/29/karen-o-soundtrack-of-my-life-yeah-yeah-yeahs |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140831054959/https://www.theguardian.com/music/2014/aug/29/karen-o-soundtrack-of-my-life-yeah-yeah-yeahs |archive-date=August 31, 2014 |access-date=March 7, 2026 |website=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> They also aimed to capture the "cocky attitude" they had whilst performing live.<ref name=":9" /> Karen O's [[staccato]] vocals became a focal point of the record, though she described her singing as "really, really, really sloshed."<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |last=True |first=Everett |author-link=Everett True |date=2002 |title=Another ancient interview with Yeah Yeah Yeahs. This one was their first ever cover story. Thought you might enjoy reading this as well. |url=https://collapseboard.com/another-ancient-interview-with-yeah-yeah-yeahs-this-one-was-their-first-ever-cover-story-thought-you-might-enjoy-reading-this-as-well/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191121173149/https://collapseboard.com/another-ancient-interview-with-yeah-yeah-yeahs-this-one-was-their-first-ever-cover-story-thought-you-might-enjoy-reading-this-as-well/ |archive-date=November 21, 2019 |access-date=March 13, 2026 |website=Collapse Board}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Berman |first=Stuart |date=August 16, 2003 |title=A conversation with Karen O, Nick Zinner, and Brian Chase of the Yeah Yeah Yeahs |magazine=[[Eye Weekly]] |page=23 |pages=}}</ref> Other influences include the rock bands [[Blondie (band)|Blondie]], [[The Jon Spencer Blues Explosion|Jon Spencer Blues Explosion]], and [[Tommy James and the Shondells]].<ref name=":11" />{{Listen

The opening track, "Bang", is about Karen O's sexual dissatisfaction with an ex-boyfriend,<ref>{{Cite web |last=True |first=Everett |author-link=Everett True |date=August 2002 |title=An ancient interview with Yeah Yeah Yeahs. Thought you might enjoy reading it. |url=http://www.collapseboard.com/features/interviews/an-ancient-interview-with-yeah-yeah-yeahs-thought-you-might-enjoy-reading-it/3/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121017110318/http://www.collapseboard.com/features/interviews/an-ancient-interview-with-yeah-yeah-yeahs-thought-you-might-enjoy-reading-it/3/ |archive-date=October 17, 2012 |access-date=March 7, 2026 |website=Collapse Board}}</ref> emphasized by the repeated lyric "As a fuck, son, you sucked!"<ref name=":1" /> The band co-wrote "Mystery Girl" with Jack Martin, which is about a sexually-promiscuous woman and her adventures.<ref name="RS" /><ref name="Pitchfork" /> "[[Art Star]]", whose lyrics satirizes [[Jet set|jet-set culture]] and the [[art world]], is the only Yeah Yeah Yeahs song with a [[spoken word]] introduction and [[Screaming in music|screaming]] vocals.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |last=Gray |first=Julia |date=June 1, 2018 |title=The 10 best Yeah Yeah Yeahs songs |url=https://stereogum.com/1999279/the-10-best-yeah-yeah-yeahs-songs/lists |access-date=March 7, 2026 |website=[[Stereogum]]}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite web |last=Frere-Jones |first=Sasha |author-link=Sasha Frere-Jones |date=February 6, 2006 |title=Positive attitude |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2006/02/13/positive-attitude |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230401151503/https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2006/02/13/positive-attitude |archive-date=April 1, 2023 |access-date=March 26, 2026 |website=[[The New Yorker]]}}</ref> "Miles Away" is about a woman that has "hurt fewer people in a better world".<ref name=":12" /> The closing track, "Our Time", is an [[anthem]] about a romance that nearly failed and perseverance,<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":8" /> which came to inspire New Yorkers after the [[September 11 attacks]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name="RSAG" />

At [[Metacritic]], which assigns a [[Standard score|normalized]] rating out of 100 to reviews from mainstream publications, ''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' received an [[Weighted arithmetic mean|average]] score of 73, indicating "generally favorable reviews".<ref name="MC" /> Critics generally praised the EP's sound; [[AllMusic]] described it as one of the most innovative releases of the 2000s [[Garage rock|garage rock revival]] at the time,<ref name="AllMusic" /> while [[Everett True]] wrote that it captured the spirit of rock n' roll.<ref name=":9" /> Karen O's performances were highlighted for additional praise, with writers for [[Blender (magazine)|''Blender'']] and ''[[CMJ]]'' describing her as "hot and sexy".<ref name=":11">{{cite magazine |last=Santangelo |first=Antonia |date=July 8, 2002 |title=Reviews |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aBw3t2fY64UC&pg=PA10-IA2 |magazine=CMJ New Music Report |page=12 |volume=72 |issue=770 |issn=0890-0795}}</ref><ref name="Blender" /> Some criticism was directed at its [[sound quality]], which was seen as limiting its potential,<ref name="RS" /> while a [[Stylus Magazine|''Stylus'']] writer found three of its five tracks unremarkable.<ref name="Stylus" /> [[Pitchfork (website)|''Pitchfork'']] noted early skepticism surrounding the rock movement but concluded that the EP demonstrated a "sharp survey" of the band's capabilities.<ref name="Pitchfork" />   

In 2002, ''[[NME]]'' ranked ''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' second on its list of the year's best singles.<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 10, 2016 |title=NME's best albums and tracks of 2002 |url=https://www.nme.com/features/2002-2-1045353 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250124234412/https://www.nme.com/features/2002-2-1045353 |archive-date=January 24, 2025 |access-date=February 12, 2026 |website=[[NME]]}}</ref> In the 2004 edition of ''[[The Rolling Stone Album Guide]]'', [[Sasha Frere-Jones]] awarded the EP four stars, writing that the band "instantly made their case for good-old-fashioned attitude"; the EP scored higher than their acclaimed debut album, ''[[Fever to Tell]]''.<ref name="RSAG" /> In 2016, ''[[Under the Radar (magazine)|Under the Radar]]'' ranked it among the best albums of its year, and said that it was essential both to the band's success and the contemporary [[Music of New York City|New York music scene]].<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Berlyant |first=Matthew |date=December 29, 2016 |title=The 15th anniversary: Yeah Yeah Yeahs' "Yeah Yeah Yeahs" EP |url=https://www.undertheradarmag.com/news/the_15th_anniversary_yeah_yeah_yeahs_yeah_yeah_yeahs_ep/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240221192539/https://www.undertheradarmag.com/news/the_15th_anniversary_yeah_yeah_yeahs_yeah_yeah_yeahs_ep/ |archive-date=February 21, 2024 |access-date=March 24, 2026 |magazine=[[Under the Radar (magazine)|Under the Radar]]}}</ref> In 2024, writers for ''[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]'' ranked it at number 42 on their list of the "100 Greatest EPs of All Time", writing that it built on the early works of contemporaries like [[the Strokes]] and [[Interpol (band)|Interpol]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=September 25, 2024 |title=The 100 Greatest EPs of All Time |url=https://www.pastemagazine.com/music/greatest-albums/the-100-greatest-eps-of-all-time |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260130195229/https://www.pastemagazine.com/music/greatest-albums/the-100-greatest-eps-of-all-time |archive-date=January 30, 2026 |access-date=March 6, 2026 |website=[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]}}</ref>

'''''Yeah Yeah Yeahs''''' (often mistitled as '''''Master''''') is the debut [[extended play]] (EP) by the American indie rock band [[Yeah Yeah Yeahs]]. After forming in 2000 and building a reputation with their live shows, Yeah Yeah Yeahs recorded and produced the EP with Jerry Teel, a member of [[Boss Hog]]. It is a record featuring the band's early [[garage rock]] and [[art punk]] influences. It was [[self-released]] on July 9, 2001, and reissued in 2002 by [[Touch and Go Records|Touch and Go]] and [[Wichita Recordings|Wichita]] in the United States and United Kingdom, respectively.  

''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' was received positively by critics and ranked by ''[[NME]]'' as the second best single of 2002. It received little attention upon release but became a [[sleeper hit]] after its reissue, topping the [[UK Independent Singles and Albums Charts|UK Indie Chart]] and exceeding sales of 71,000 units in the United States by the end of the decade. In 2024, [[Paste (magazine)|''Paste'']] ranked it among the greatest EPs ever made.

''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' consists of five tracks and runs for 13 minutes and 52 seconds.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" /> The songs were written by Karen O and its music was composed by the band.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rogers |first=Jude |author-link=Jude Rogers |date=March 14, 2019 |title='I just wanted to write a love song that stands the test of time': Karen O on her best work |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2019/mar/14/all-i-ever-wanted-to-do-was-write-a-love-song-that-stands-the-test-of-time-karen-o-on-her-best-songs |access-date=March 13, 2026 |website=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> The rock band [[ESG (band)|ESG]] served as a primary influence for the EP, with the band attempting to recreate their sound "with guitar instead of bass."<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 29, 2014 |title=Karen O: soundtrack of my life |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2014/aug/29/karen-o-soundtrack-of-my-life-yeah-yeah-yeahs |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140831054959/https://www.theguardian.com/music/2014/aug/29/karen-o-soundtrack-of-my-life-yeah-yeah-yeahs |archive-date=August 31, 2014 |access-date=March 7, 2026 |website=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> They also aimed to capture the "cocky attitude" they had whilst performing live.<ref name=":9" /> Karen O's [[staccato]] vocals became a focal point of the record, though she described her singing as "really, really, really sloshed."<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |last=True |first=Everett |author-link=Everett True |date=2002 |title=Another ancient interview with Yeah Yeah Yeahs. The opening track, "Bang", is about Karen O's sexual dissatisfaction with an ex-boyfriend,<ref>{{Cite web |last=True |first=Everett |author-link=Everett True |date=August 2002 |title=An ancient interview with Yeah Yeah Yeahs. Thought you might enjoy reading it. |url=http://www.collapseboard.com/features/interviews/an-ancient-interview-with-yeah-yeah-yeahs-thought-you-might-enjoy-reading-it/3/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121017110318/http://www.collapseboard.com/features/interviews/an-ancient-interview-with-yeah-yeah-yeahs-thought-you-might-enjoy-reading-it/3/ |archive-date=October 17, 2012 |access-date=March 7, 2026 |website=Collapse Board}}</ref> emphasized by the repeated lyric "As a fuck, son, you sucked!"<ref name=":1" /> The band co-wrote "Mystery Girl" with Jack Martin, which is about a sexually-promiscuous woman and her adventures.<ref name="RS" /><ref name="Pitchfork" /> "[[Art Star]]", whose lyrics satirizes [[Jet set|jet-set culture]] and the [[art world]], is the only Yeah Yeah Yeahs song with a [[spoken word]] introduction and [[Screaming in music|screaming]] vocals.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |last=Gray |first=Julia |date=June 1, 2018 |title=The 10 best Yeah Yeah Yeahs songs |url=https://stereogum.com/1999279/the-10-best-yeah-yeah-yeahs-songs/lists |access-date=March 7, 2026 |website=[[Stereogum]]}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite web |last=Frere-Jones |first=Sasha |author-link=Sasha Frere-Jones |date=February 6, 2006 |title=Positive attitude |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2006/02/13/positive-attitude |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230401151503/https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2006/02/13/positive-attitude |archive-date=April 1, 2023 |access-date=March 26, 2026 |website=[[The New Yorker]]}}</ref> "Miles Away" is about a woman that has "hurt fewer people in a better world".<ref name=":12" /> The closing track, "Our Time", is an [[anthem]] about a romance that nearly failed and perseverance,<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":8" /> which came to inspire New Yorkers after the [[September 11 attacks]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name="RSAG" />

'''''Yeah Yeah Yeahs''''' (often mistitled as '''''Master''''') is the debut [[extended play]] (EP) by the American indie rock band [[Yeah Yeah Yeahs]]. After forming in 2000 and building a reputation with their live shows, Yeah Yeah Yeahs recorded and produced the EP with Jerry Teel, a member of [[Boss Hog]]. It is a record featuring the band's early [[garage rock]] and [[art punk]] influences. It was [[self-released]] on July 9, 2001, and reissued in 2002 by [[Touch and Go Records|Touch and Go]] and [[Wichita Recordings|Wichita]] in the United States and United Kingdom, respectively.  

''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' was received positively by critics and ranked by ''[[NME]]'' as the second best single of 2002. It received little attention upon release but became a [[sleeper hit]] after its reissue, topping the [[UK Independent Singles and Albums Charts|UK Indie Chart]] and exceeding sales of 71,000 units in the United States by the end of the decade. In 2024, [[Paste (magazine)|''Paste'']] ranked it among the greatest EPs ever made. 

== Background and recording ==
The singer/songwriter [[Karen O]] and guitarist [[Nick Zinner]] founded the acoustic duo Unitard in 2000. They changed their name that year to Yeah Yeah Yeahs and shifted to a "trashy, punky, [and] grimy" sound inspired by the contemporary Ohio music scene.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web |last=Houghton ''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' was recorded at [[Avenue B (Manhattan)|Avenue B]]'s Funhouse Recording Studio with Teel—which doubled as their rehearsal space—while Chuck Scott [[Mastering (audio)|mastered]] it at Soundoptik in New York City.{{Sfn|Goodman|2017|p=229}}<ref name=":0" /> The artwork and packaging was designed by the band and Crispin.<ref name=":0" /> The front cover is a [[close-up]] of a topless Karen O, and the back cover features three different [[Selfie|self-photographs]] of her, Zinner and Chase.<ref name=":0" /> Although it is self-titled, the EP is sometimes mistitled as ''Master'' due to the necklace Karen O wears on the cover.<ref name=":1" />
== Music and lyrics ==
''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' consists of five tracks and runs for 13 minutes and 52 seconds.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" /> The songs were written by Karen O and its music was composed by the band.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rogers |first=Jude |author-link=Jude Rogers |date=March 14, 2019 |title='I just wanted to write a love song that stands the test of time': Karen O on her best work |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2019/mar/14/all-i-ever-wanted-to-do-was-write-a-love-song-that-stands-the-test-of-time-karen-o-on-her-best-songs |access-date=March 13, 2026 |website=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> The rock band [[ESG (band)|ESG]] served as a primary influence for the EP, with the band attempting to recreate their sound "with guitar instead of bass."<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 29, 2014 |title=Karen O: soundtrack of my life |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2014/aug/29/karen-o-soundtrack-of-my-life-yeah-yeah-yeahs |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140831054959/https://www.theguardian.com/music/2014/aug/29/karen-o-soundtrack-of-my-life-yeah-yeah-yeahs |archive-date=August 31, 2014 |access-date=March 7, 2026 |website=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> They also aimed to capture the "cocky attitude" they had whilst performing live.<ref name=":9" /> Karen O's [[staccato]] vocals became a focal point of the record, though she described her singing as "really, really, really sloshed."<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |last=True |first=Everett |author-link=Everett True |date=2002 |title=Another ancient interview with Yeah Yeah Yeahs. This one was their first ever cover story. Thought you might enjoy reading this as well. |url=https://collapseboard.com/another-ancient-interview-with-yeah-yeah-yeahs-this-one-was-their-first-ever-cover-story-thought-you-might-enjoy-reading-this-as-well/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191121173149/https://collapseboard.com/another-ancient-interview-with-yeah-yeah-yeahs-this-one-was-their-first-ever-cover-story-thought-you-might-enjoy-reading-this-as-well/ |archive-date=November 21, 2019 |access-date=March 13, 2026 |website=Collapse Board}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Berman |first=Stuart |date=August 16, 2003 |title=A conversation with Karen O, Nick Zinner, and Brian Chase of the Yeah Yeah Yeahs |magazine=[[Eye Weekly]] |page=23 |pages=}}</ref> Other influences include the rock bands [[Blondie (band)|Blondie]], [[The Jon Spencer Blues Explosion|Jon Spencer Blues Explosion]], and [[Tommy James and the Shondells]].<ref name=":11" />{{Listen

The opening track, "Bang", is about Karen O's sexual dissatisfaction with an ex-boyfriend,<ref>{{Cite web |last=True |first=Everett |author-link=Everett True |date=August 2002 |title=An ancient interview with Yeah Yeah Yeahs. Thought you might enjoy reading it. |url=http://www.collapseboard.com/features/interviews/an-ancient-interview-with-yeah-yeah-yeahs-thought-you-might-enjoy-reading-it/3/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121017110318/http://www.collapseboard.com/features/interviews/an-ancient-interview-with-yeah-yeah-yeahs-thought-you-might-enjoy-reading-it/3/ |archive-date=October 17, 2012 |access-date=March 7, 2026 |website=Collapse Board}}</ref> emphasized by the repeated lyric "As a fuck, son, you sucked!"<ref name=":1" /> The band co-wrote "Mystery Girl" with Jack Martin, which is about a sexually-promiscuous woman and her adventures.<ref name="RS" /><ref name="Pitchfork" /> "[[Art Star]]", whose lyrics satirizes [[Jet set|jet-set culture]] and the [[art world]], is the only Yeah Yeah Yeahs song with a [[spoken word]] introduction and [[Screaming in music|screaming]] vocals.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |last=Gray |first=Julia |date=June 1, 2018 |title=The 10 best Yeah Yeah Yeahs songs |url=https://stereogum.com/1999279/the-10-best-yeah-yeah-yeahs-songs/lists |access-date=March 7, 2026 |website=[[Stereogum]]}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite web |last=Frere-Jones |first=Sasha |author-link=Sasha Frere-Jones |date=February 6, 2006 |title=Positive attitude |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2006/02/13/positive-attitude |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230401151503/https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2006/02/13/positive-attitude |archive-date=April 1, 2023 |access-date=March 26, 2026 |website=[[The New Yorker]]}}</ref> "Miles Away" is about a woman that has "hurt fewer people in a better world".<ref name=":12" /> The closing track, "Our Time", is an [[anthem]] about a romance that nearly failed and perseverance,<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":8" /> which came to inspire New Yorkers after the [[September 11 attacks]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name="RSAG" />

At [[Metacritic]], which assigns a [[Standard score|normalized]] rating out of 100 to reviews from mainstream publications, ''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' received an [[Weighted arithmetic mean|average]] score of 73, indicating "generally favorable reviews".<ref name="MC" /> Critics generally praised the EP's sound; [[AllMusic]] described it as one of the most innovative releases of the 2000s [[Garage rock|garage rock revival]] at the time,<ref name="AllMusic" /> while [[Everett True]] wrote that it captured the spirit of rock n' roll.<ref name=":9" /> Karen O's performances were highlighted for additional praise, with writers for [[Blender (magazine)|''Blender'']] and ''[[CMJ]]'' describing her as "hot and sexy".<ref name=":11">{{cite magazine |last=Santangelo |first=Antonia |date=July 8, 2002 |title=Reviews |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aBw3t2fY64UC&pg=PA10-IA2 |magazine=CMJ New Music Report |page=12 |volume=72 |issue=770 |issn=0890-0795}}</ref><ref name="Blender" /> Some criticism was directed at its [[sound quality]], which was seen as limiting its potential,<ref name="RS" /> while a [[Stylus Magazine|''Stylus'']] writer found three of its five tracks unremarkable.<ref name="Stylus" /> [[Pitchfork (website)|''Pitchfork'']] noted early skepticism surrounding the rock movement but concluded that the EP demonstrated a "sharp survey" of the band's capabilities.<ref name="Pitchfork" />   

In 2002, ''[[NME]]'' ranked ''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' second on its list of the year's best singles.<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 10, 2016 |title=NME's best albums and tracks of 2002 |url=https://www.nme.com/features/2002-2-1045353 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250124234412/https://www.nme.com/features/2002-2-1045353 |archive-date=January 24, 2025 |access-date=February 12, 2026 |website=[[NME]]}}</ref> In the 2004 edition of ''[[The Rolling Stone Album Guide]]'', [[Sasha Frere-Jones]] awarded the EP four stars, writing that the band "instantly made their case for good-old-fashioned attitude"; the EP scored higher than their acclaimed debut album, ''[[Fever to Tell]]''.<ref name="RSAG" /> In 2016, ''[[Under the Radar (magazine)|Under the Radar]]'' ranked it among the best albums of its year, and said that it was essential both to the band's success and the contemporary [[Music of New York City|New York music scene]].<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Berlyant |first=Matthew |date=December 29, 2016 |title=The 15th anniversary: Yeah Yeah Yeahs' "Yeah Yeah Yeahs" EP |url=https://www.undertheradarmag.com/news/the_15th_anniversary_yeah_yeah_yeahs_yeah_yeah_yeahs_ep/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240221192539/https://www.undertheradarmag.com/news/the_15th_anniversary_yeah_yeah_yeahs_yeah_yeah_yeahs_ep/ |archive-date=February 21, 2024 |access-date=March 24, 2026 |magazine=[[Under the Radar (magazine)|Under the Radar]]}}</ref> In 2024, writers for ''[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]'' ranked it at number 42 on their list of the "100 Greatest EPs of All Time", writing that it built on the early works of contemporaries like [[the Strokes]] and [[Interpol (band)|Interpol]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=September 25, 2024 |title=The 100 Greatest EPs of All Time |url=https://www.pastemagazine.com/music/greatest-albums/the-100-greatest-eps-of-all-time |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260130195229/https://www.pastemagazine.com/music/greatest-albums/the-100-greatest-eps-of-all-time |archive-date=January 30, 2026 |access-date=March 6, 2026 |website=[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]}}</ref>

'''''Yeah Yeah Yeahs''''' (often mistitled as '''''Master''''') is the debut [[extended play]] (EP) by the American indie rock band [[Yeah Yeah Yeahs]]. After forming in 2000 and building a reputation with their live shows, Yeah Yeah Yeahs recorded and produced the EP with Jerry Teel, a member of [[Boss Hog]]. It is a record featuring the band's early [[garage rock]] and [[art punk]] influences. It was [[self-released]] on July 9, 2001, and reissued in 2002 by [[Touch and Go Records|Touch and Go]] and [[Wichita Recordings|Wichita]] in the United States and United Kingdom, respectively.  

''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' was received positively by critics and ranked by ''[[NME]]'' as the second best single of 2002. It received little attention upon release but became a [[sleeper hit]] after its reissue, topping the [[UK Independent Singles and Albums Charts|UK Indie Chart]] and exceeding sales of 71,000 units in the United States by the end of the decade. In 2024, [[Paste (magazine)|''Paste'']] ranked it among the greatest EPs ever made. 

== Background and recording ==
The singer/songwriter [[Karen O]] and guitarist [[Nick Zinner]] founded the acoustic duo Unitard in 2000. They changed their name that year to Yeah Yeah Yeahs and shifted to a "trashy, punky, [and] grimy" sound inspired by the contemporary Ohio music scene.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web |last=Houghton |first=Cillea |date=April 4, 2023 |title=Behind the New York City-inspired band name: Yeah Yeah Yeahs |url=https://americansongwriter.com/behind-the-new-york-city-inspired-band-name-yeah-yeah-yeahs/ Guardian]]}}</ref> In September 2000, they added drummer [[Brian Chase]] to the lineup.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Brazeal |first=Anne |date=September 8, 2014 |title=Original buzz: Yeah Yeah Yeahs |url=https://www.thefader.com/2014/09/08/yeah-yeah-yeahs-interview-2003 |url-status=live Fader]]}}</ref> By early 2001, the band earned a live following.<ref name="RS" /><ref name="timesonline20092">{{cite web |last=McLean |first=Craig |date=June 13, 2009 |title=Yeah Yeah Yeahs: why fans of the art-punk trio can't say no |url=http://entertainment.timesonline.co.uk/tol/arts_and_entertainment/music/article6485717.ece |url-status= However, they ultimately developed the demo into their debut EP, a decision that Zinner attributes to their desire to share their music.{{Sfn|Goodman|2017|p=229}} 

''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' was recorded at [[Avenue B (Manhattan)|Avenue B]]'s Funhouse Recording Studio with Teel—which doubled as their rehearsal space—while Chuck Scott [[Mastering (audio)|mastered]] it at Soundoptik in New York City.{{Sfn|Goodman|2017|p=229}}<ref name=":0" /> The artwork and packaging was designed by the band and Crispin.<ref name=":0" /> The front cover is a [[close-up]] of a topless Karen O, and the back cover features three different [[Selfie|self-photographs]] of her, Zinner and Chase.<ref name=":0" /> Although it is self-titled, the EP is sometimes mistitled as ''Master'' due to the necklace Karen O wears on the cover.<ref name=":1" />
== Music and lyrics ==
''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' consists of five tracks and runs for 13 minutes and 52 seconds.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" /> The songs were written by Karen O and its music was composed by the band.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rogers |first=Jude |author-link=Jude Rogers |date=March 14, 2019 |title='I just wanted to write a love song that stands the test of time': Karen O on her best work |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2019/mar/14/all-i-ever-wanted-to-do-was-write-a-love-song-that-stands-the-test-of-time-karen-o-on-her-best-songs |access-date=March 13, 2026 |website=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> The rock band [[ESG (band)|ESG]] served as a primary influence for the EP, with the band attempting to recreate their sound "with guitar instead of bass."<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 29, 2014 |title=Karen O: soundtrack of my life |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2014/aug/29/karen-o-soundtrack-of-my-life-yeah-yeah-yeahs |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140831054959/https://www.theguardian.com/music/2014/aug/29/karen-o-soundtrack-of-my-life-yeah-yeah-yeahs |archive-date=August 31, 2014 |access-date=March 7, 2026 |website=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> They also aimed to capture the "cocky attitude" they had whilst performing live.<ref name=":9" /> Karen O's [[staccato]] vocals became a focal point of the record, though she described her singing as "really, really, really sloshed."<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |last=True |first=Everett |author-link=Everett True |date=2002 |title=Another ancient interview with Yeah Yeah Yeahs. This one was their first ever cover story. Thought you might enjoy reading this as well. |url=https://collapseboard.com/another-ancient-interview-with-yeah-yeah-yeahs-this-one-was-their-first-ever-cover-story-thought-you-might-enjoy-reading-this-as-well/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191121173149/https://collapseboard.com/another-ancient-interview-with-yeah-yeah-yeahs-this-one-was-their-first-ever-cover-story-thought-you-might-enjoy-reading-this-as-well/ |archive-date=November 21, 2019 |access-date=March 13, 2026 |website=Collapse Board}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Berman |first=Stuart |date=August 16, 2003 |title=A conversation with Karen O, Nick Zinner, and Brian Chase of the Yeah Yeah Yeahs |magazine=[[Eye Weekly]] |page=23 |pages=}}</ref> Other influences include the rock bands [[Blondie (band)|Blondie]], [[The Jon Spencer Blues Explosion|Jon Spencer Blues Explosion]], and [[Tommy James and the Shondells]].<ref name=":11" />{{Listen

The opening track, "Bang", is about Karen O's sexual dissatisfaction with an ex-boyfriend,<ref>{{Cite web |last=True |first=Everett |author-link=Everett True |date=August 2002 |title=An ancient interview with Yeah Yeah Yeahs. Thought you might enjoy reading it. |url=http://www.collapseboard.com/features/interviews/an-ancient-interview-with-yeah-yeah-yeahs-thought-you-might-enjoy-reading-it/3/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121017110318/http://www.collapseboard.com/features/interviews/an-ancient-interview-with-yeah-yeah-yeahs-thought-you-might-enjoy-reading-it/3/ |archive-date=October 17, 2012 |access-date=March 7, 2026 |website=Collapse Board}}</ref> emphasized by the repeated lyric "As a fuck, son, you sucked!"<ref name=":1" /> The band co-wrote "Mystery Girl" with Jack Martin, which is about a sexually-promiscuous woman and her adventures.<ref name="RS" /><ref name="Pitchfork" /> "[[Art Star]]", whose lyrics satirizes [[Jet set|jet-set culture]] and the [[art world]], is the only Yeah Yeah Yeahs song with a [[spoken word]] introduction and [[Screaming in music|screaming]] vocals.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |last=Gray |first=Julia |date=June 1, 2018 |title=The 10 best Yeah Yeah Yeahs songs |url=https://stereogum.com/1999279/the-10-best-yeah-yeah-yeahs-songs/lists |access-date=March 7, 2026 |website=[[Stereogum]]}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite web |last=Frere-Jones |first=Sasha |author-link=Sasha Frere-Jones |date=February 6, 2006 |title=Positive attitude |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2006/02/13/positive-attitude |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230401151503/https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2006/02/13/positive-attitude |archive-date=April 1, 2023 |access-date=March 26, 2026 |website=[[The New Yorker]]}}</ref> "Miles Away" is about a woman that has "hurt fewer people in a better world".<ref name=":12" /> The closing track, "Our Time", is an [[anthem]] about a romance that nearly failed and perseverance,<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":8" /> which came to inspire New Yorkers after the [[September 11 attacks]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name="RSAG" />

At [[Metacritic]], which assigns a [[Standard score|normalized]] rating out of 100 to reviews from mainstream publications, ''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' received an [[Weighted arithmetic mean|average]] score of 73, indicating "generally favorable reviews".<ref name="MC" /> Critics generally praised the EP's sound; [[AllMusic]] described it as one of the most innovative releases of the 2000s [[Garage rock|garage rock revival]] at the time,<ref name="AllMusic" /> while [[Everett True]] wrote that it captured the spirit of rock n' roll.<ref name=":9" /> Karen O's performances were highlighted for additional praise, with writers for [[Blender (magazine)|''Blender'']] and ''[[CMJ]]'' describing her as "hot and sexy".<ref name=":11">{{cite magazine |last=Santangelo |first=Antonia |date=July 8, 2002 |title=Reviews |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aBw3t2fY64UC&pg=PA10-IA2 |magazine=CMJ New Music Report |page=12 |volume=72 |issue=770 |issn=0890-0795}}</ref><ref name="Blender" /> Some criticism was directed at its [[sound quality]], which was seen as limiting its potential,<ref name="RS" /> while a [[Stylus Magazine|''Stylus'']] writer found three of its five tracks unremarkable.<ref name="Stylus" /> [[Pitchfork (website)|''Pitchfork'']] noted early skepticism surrounding the rock movement but concluded that the EP demonstrated a "sharp survey" of the band's capabilities.<ref name="Pitchfork" />   

In 2002, ''[[NME]]'' ranked ''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' second on its list of the year's best singles.<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 10, 2016 |title=NME's best albums and tracks of 2002 |url=https://www.nme.com/features/2002-2-1045353 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250124234412/https://www.nme.com/features/2002-2-1045353 |archive-date=January 24, 2025 |access-date=February 12, 2026 |website=[[NME]]}}</ref> In the 2004 edition of ''[[The Rolling Stone Album Guide]]'', [[Sasha Frere-Jones]] awarded the EP four stars, writing that the band "instantly made their case for good-old-fashioned attitude"; the EP scored higher than their acclaimed debut album, ''[[Fever to Tell]]''.<ref name="RSAG" /> In 2016, ''[[Under the Radar (magazine)|Under the Radar]]'' ranked it among the best albums of its year, and said that it was essential both to the band's success and the contemporary [[Music of New York City|New York music scene]].<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Berlyant |first=Matthew |date=December 29, 2016 |title=The 15th anniversary: Yeah Yeah Yeahs' "Yeah Yeah Yeahs" EP |url=https://www.undertheradarmag.com/news/the_15th_anniversary_yeah_yeah_yeahs_yeah_yeah_yeahs_ep/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240221192539/https://www.undertheradarmag.com/news/the_15th_anniversary_yeah_yeah_yeahs_yeah_yeah_yeahs_ep/ |archive-date=February 21, 2024 |access-date=March 24, 2026 |magazine=[[Under the Radar (magazine)|Under the Radar]]}}</ref> In 2024, writers for ''[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]'' ranked it at number 42 on their list of the "100 Greatest EPs of All Time", writing that it built on the early works of contemporaries like [[the Strokes]] and [[Interpol (band)|Interpol]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=September 25, 2024 |title=The 100 Greatest EPs of All Time |url=https://www.pastemagazine.com/music/greatest-albums/the-100-greatest-eps-of-all-time |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260130195229/https://www.pastemagazine.com/music/greatest-albums/the-100-greatest-eps-of-all-time |archive-date=January 30, 2026 |access-date=March 6, 2026 |website=[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]}}</ref>

'''''Yeah Yeah Yeahs''''' (often mistitled as '''''Master''''') is the debut [[extended play]] (EP) by the American indie rock band [[Yeah Yeah Yeahs]]. After forming in 2000 and building a reputation with their live shows, Yeah Yeah Yeahs recorded and produced the EP with Jerry Teel, a member of [[Boss Hog]]. It is a record featuring the band's early [[garage rock]] and [[art punk]] influences. It was [[self-released]] on July 9, 2001, and reissued in 2002 by [[Touch and Go Records|Touch and Go]] and other [[Independent record label|independent labels]] worldwide.  

''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' was received positively by critics and ranked by ''[[NME]]'' as the second best single of 2002. It received little attention upon release but became a [[sleeper hit]] after its reissue, topping the [[UK Independent Singles and Albums Charts|UK Indie Chart]] and exceeding sales of 71,000 units in the United States by the end of the decade. In 2024, [[Paste (magazine)|''Paste'']] ranked it among the greatest EPs ever made. 

== Background and recording ==
The singer/songwriter [[Karen O]] and guitarist [[Nick Zinner]] founded the acoustic duo Unitard in 2000. They changed their name that year to Yeah Yeah Yeahs and shifted to a "trashy, punky, [and] grimy" sound inspired by the contemporary Ohio music scene.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web |last=Houghton |url=https://www.thefader.com/2014/09/08/yeah-yeah-yeahs-interview-2003 |url-status=live ''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' was recorded at [[Avenue B (Manhattan)|Avenue B]]'s Funhouse Recording Studio with Teel—which doubled as their rehearsal space—while Chuck Scott [[Mastering (audio)|mastered]] it at Soundoptik in New York City.{{Sfn|Goodman|2017|p=229}}<ref name=":0" /> The artwork and packaging was designed by the band and Crispin.<ref name=":0" /> The front cover is a [[close-up]] of a topless Karen O, and the back cover features three different [[Selfie|self-photographs]] of her, Zinner and Chase.<ref name=":0" /> Although it is self-titled, the EP is sometimes mistitled as ''Master'' due to the necklace Karen O wears on the cover.<ref name=":1" />
== Music and lyrics ==
''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' consists of five tracks and runs for 13 minutes and 52 seconds.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" /> The songs were written by Karen O and its music was composed by the band.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rogers |first=Jude |author-link=Jude Rogers |date=March 14, 2019 |title='I just wanted to write a love song that stands the test of time': Karen O on her best work |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2019/mar/14/all-i-ever-wanted-to-do-was-write-a-love-song-that-stands-the-test-of-time-karen-o-on-her-best-songs |access-date=March 13, 2026 |website=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> The rock band [[ESG (band)|ESG]] served as a primary influence for the EP, with the band attempting to recreate their sound "with guitar instead of bass."<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 29, 2014 |title=Karen O: soundtrack of my life |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2014/aug/29/karen-o-soundtrack-of-my-life-yeah-yeah-yeahs |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140831054959/https://www.theguardian.com/music/2014/aug/29/karen-o-soundtrack-of-my-life-yeah-yeah-yeahs |archive-date=August 31, 2014 |access-date=March 7, 2026 |website=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> They also aimed to capture the "cocky attitude" they had whilst performing live.<ref name=":9" /> Karen O's [[staccato]] vocals became a focal point of the record, though she described her singing as "really, really, really sloshed."<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |last=True |first=Everett |author-link=Everett True |date=2002 |title=Another ancient interview with Yeah Yeah Yeahs. This one was their first ever cover story. Thought you might enjoy reading this as well. |url=https://collapseboard.com/another-ancient-interview-with-yeah-yeah-yeahs-this-one-was-their-first-ever-cover-story-thought-you-might-enjoy-reading-this-as-well/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191121173149/https://collapseboard.com/another-ancient-interview-with-yeah-yeah-yeahs-this-one-was-their-first-ever-cover-story-thought-you-might-enjoy-reading-this-as-well/ |archive-date=November 21, 2019 |access-date=March 13, 2026 |website=Collapse Board}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Berman |first=Stuart |date=August 16, 2003 |title=A conversation with Karen O, Nick Zinner, and Brian Chase of the Yeah Yeah Yeahs |magazine=[[Eye Weekly]] |page=23 |pages=}}</ref> Other influences include the rock bands [[Blondie (band)|Blondie]], [[The Jon Spencer Blues Explosion|Jon Spencer Blues Explosion]], and [[Tommy James and the Shondells]].<ref name=":11" />{{Listen

The opening track, "Bang", is about Karen O's sexual dissatisfaction with an ex-boyfriend,<ref>{{Cite web |last=True |first=Everett |author-link=Everett True |date=August 2002 |title=An ancient interview with Yeah Yeah Yeahs. Thought you might enjoy reading it. |url=http://www.collapseboard.com/features/interviews/an-ancient-interview-with-yeah-yeah-yeahs-thought-you-might-enjoy-reading-it/3/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121017110318/http://www.collapseboard.com/features/interviews/an-ancient-interview-with-yeah-yeah-yeahs-thought-you-might-enjoy-reading-it/3/ |archive-date=October 17, 2012 |access-date=March 7, 2026 |website=Collapse Board}}</ref> emphasized by the repeated lyric "As a fuck, son, you sucked!"<ref name=":1" /> The band co-wrote "Mystery Girl" with Jack Martin, which is about a sexually-promiscuous woman and her adventures.<ref name="RS" /><ref name="Pitchfork" /> "[[Art Star]]", whose lyrics satirizes [[Jet set|jet-set culture]] and the [[art world]], is the only Yeah Yeah Yeahs song with a [[spoken word]] introduction and [[Screaming in music|screaming]] vocals.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |last=Gray |first=Julia |date=June 1, 2018 |title=The 10 best Yeah Yeah Yeahs songs |url=https://stereogum.com/1999279/the-10-best-yeah-yeah-yeahs-songs/lists |access-date=March 7, 2026 |website=[[Stereogum]]}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite web |last=Frere-Jones |first=Sasha |author-link=Sasha Frere-Jones |date=February 6, 2006 |title=Positive attitude |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2006/02/13/positive-attitude |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230401151503/https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2006/02/13/positive-attitude |archive-date=April 1, 2023 |access-date=March 26, 2026 |website=[[The New Yorker]]}}</ref> "Miles Away" is about a woman that has "hurt fewer people in a better world".<ref name=":12" /> The closing track, "Our Time", is an [[anthem]] about a romance that nearly failed and perseverance,<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":8" /> which came to inspire New Yorkers after the [[September 11 attacks]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name="RSAG" />

At [[Metacritic]], which assigns a [[Standard score|normalized]] rating out of 100 to reviews from mainstream publications, ''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' received an [[Weighted arithmetic mean|average]] score of 73, indicating "generally favorable reviews".<ref name="MC" /> Critics generally praised the EP's sound; [[AllMusic]] described it as one of the most innovative releases of the 2000s [[Garage rock|garage rock revival]] at the time,<ref name="AllMusic" /> while [[Everett True]] wrote that it captured the spirit of rock n' roll.<ref name=":9" /> Karen O's performances were highlighted for additional praise, with writers for [[Blender (magazine)|''Blender'']] and ''[[CMJ]]'' describing her as "hot and sexy".<ref name=":11">{{cite magazine |last=Santangelo |first=Antonia |date=July 8, 2002 |title=Reviews |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aBw3t2fY64UC&pg=PA10-IA2 |magazine=CMJ New Music Report |page=12 |volume=72 |issue=770 |issn=0890-0795}}</ref><ref name="Blender" /> Some criticism was directed at its [[sound quality]], which was seen as limiting its potential,<ref name="RS" /> while a [[Stylus Magazine|''Stylus'']] writer found three of its five tracks unremarkable.<ref name="Stylus" /> [[Pitchfork (website)|''Pitchfork'']] noted early skepticism surrounding the rock movement but concluded that the EP demonstrated a "sharp survey" of the band's capabilities.<ref name="Pitchfork" />   

In 2002, ''[[NME]]'' ranked ''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' second on its list of the year's best singles.<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 10, 2016 |title=NME's best albums and tracks of 2002 |url=https://www.nme.com/features/2002-2-1045353 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250124234412/https://www.nme.com/features/2002-2-1045353 |archive-date=January 24, 2025 |access-date=February 12, 2026 |website=[[NME]]}}</ref> In the 2004 edition of ''[[The Rolling Stone Album Guide]]'', [[Sasha Frere-Jones]] awarded the EP four stars, writing that the band "instantly made their case for good-old-fashioned attitude"; the EP scored higher than their acclaimed debut album, ''[[Fever to Tell]]''.<ref name="RSAG" /> In 2016, ''[[Under the Radar (magazine)|Under the Radar]]'' ranked it among the best albums of its year, and said that it was essential both to the band's success and the contemporary [[Music of New York City|New York music scene]].<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Berlyant |first=Matthew |date=December 29, 2016 |title=The 15th anniversary: Yeah Yeah Yeahs' "Yeah Yeah Yeahs" EP |url=https://www.undertheradarmag.com/news/the_15th_anniversary_yeah_yeah_yeahs_yeah_yeah_yeahs_ep/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240221192539/https://www.undertheradarmag.com/news/the_15th_anniversary_yeah_yeah_yeahs_yeah_yeah_yeahs_ep/ |archive-date=February 21, 2024 |access-date=March 24, 2026 |magazine=[[Under the Radar (magazine)|Under the Radar]]}}</ref> In 2024, writers for ''[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]'' ranked it at number 42 on their list of the "100 Greatest EPs of All Time", writing that it built on the early works of contemporaries like [[the Strokes]] and [[Interpol (band)|Interpol]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=September 25, 2024 |title=The 100 Greatest EPs of All Time |url=https://www.pastemagazine.com/music/greatest-albums/the-100-greatest-eps-of-all-time |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260130195229/https://www.pastemagazine.com/music/greatest-albums/the-100-greatest-eps-of-all-time |archive-date=January 30, 2026 |access-date=March 6, 2026 |website=[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]}}</ref>

'''''Yeah Yeah Yeahs''''' (often mistitled as '''''Master''''') is the debut [[extended play]] (EP) by the American indie rock band [[Yeah Yeah Yeahs]]. After forming in 2000 and building a reputation with their live shows, Yeah Yeah Yeahs recorded and produced the EP with Jerry Teel, a member of [[Boss Hog]]. It is a record featuring the band's early [[garage rock]] and [[art punk]] influences. It was [[self-released]] on July 9, 2001, and reissued in 2002 by [[Touch and Go Records|Touch and Go]] and other [[Independent record label|independent labels]] worldwide.  

''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' was received positively by critics and ranked by ''[[NME]]'' as the second best single of 2002. It received little attention upon release but became a [[sleeper hit]] after its reissue, topping the [[UK Independent Singles and Albums Charts|UK Indie Chart]] and exceeding sales of 71,000 units in the United States by the end of the decade. In 2024, [[Paste (magazine)|''Paste'']] ranked it among the greatest EPs ever made. 

== Background and recording ==
The singer/songwriter [[Karen O]] and guitarist [[Nick Zinner]] founded the acoustic duo Unitard in 2000. They changed their name that year to Yeah Yeah Yeahs and shifted to a "trashy, punky, [and] grimy" sound inspired by the contemporary Ohio music scene.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web |last=Houghton |url=https://www.thefader.com/2014/09/08/yeah-yeah-yeahs-interview-2003 |url-status=live ''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' was recorded at [[Avenue B (Manhattan)|Avenue B]]'s Funhouse Recording Studio with Teel—which doubled as their rehearsal space—while Chuck Scott [[Mastering (audio)|mastered]] it at Soundoptik in New York City.{{Sfn|Goodman|2017|p=229}}<ref name=":0" /> The artwork and packaging was designed by the band and Crispin.<ref name=":0" /> The front cover is a [[close-up]] of a topless Karen O, and the back cover features three different [[Selfie|self-photographs]] of her, Zinner and Chase.<ref name=":0" /> Although it is self-titled, the EP is sometimes mistitled as ''Master'' due to the necklace Karen O wears on the cover.<ref name=":1" />
== Music and lyrics ==
''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' consists of five tracks and runs for 13 minutes and 52 seconds.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" /> The songs were written by Karen O and its music was composed by the band.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rogers |first=Jude |author-link=Jude Rogers |date=March 14, 2019 |title='I just wanted to write a love song that stands the test of time': Karen O on her best work |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2019/mar/14/all-i-ever-wanted-to-do-was-write-a-love-song-that-stands-the-test-of-time-karen-o-on-her-best-songs |access-date=March 13, 2026 |website=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> The rock band [[ESG (band)|ESG]] served as a primary influence for the EP, with the band attempting to recreate their sound "with guitar instead of bass."<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 29, 2014 |title=Karen O: soundtrack of my life |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2014/aug/29/karen-o-soundtrack-of-my-life-yeah-yeah-yeahs |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140831054959/https://www.theguardian.com/music/2014/aug/29/karen-o-soundtrack-of-my-life-yeah-yeah-yeahs |archive-date=August 31, 2014 |access-date=March 7, 2026 |website=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> They also aimed to capture the "cocky attitude" they had whilst performing live.<ref name=":9" /> Karen O's [[staccato]] vocals became a focal point of the record, though she described her singing as "really, really, really sloshed."<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |last=True |first=Everett |author-link=Everett True |date=2002 |title=Another ancient interview with Yeah Yeah Yeahs. This one was their first ever cover story. Thought you might enjoy reading this as well. |url=https://collapseboard.com/another-ancient-interview-with-yeah-yeah-yeahs-this-one-was-their-first-ever-cover-story-thought-you-might-enjoy-reading-this-as-well/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191121173149/https://collapseboard.com/another-ancient-interview-with-yeah-yeah-yeahs-this-one-was-their-first-ever-cover-story-thought-you-might-enjoy-reading-this-as-well/ |archive-date=November 21, 2019 |access-date=March 13, 2026 |website=Collapse Board}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Berman |first=Stuart |date=August 16, 2003 |title=A conversation with Karen O, Nick Zinner, and Brian Chase of the Yeah Yeah Yeahs |magazine=[[Eye Weekly]] |page=23 |pages=}}</ref> Other influences include the rock bands [[Blondie (band)|Blondie]], [[The Jon Spencer Blues Explosion|Jon Spencer Blues Explosion]], and [[Tommy James and the Shondells]].<ref name=":11" />{{Listen

The opening track, "Bang", is about Karen O's sexual dissatisfaction with an ex-boyfriend,<ref>{{Cite web |last=True |first=Everett |author-link=Everett True |date=August 2002 |title=An ancient interview with Yeah Yeah Yeahs. Thought you might enjoy reading it. |url=http://www.collapseboard.com/features/interviews/an-ancient-interview-with-yeah-yeah-yeahs-thought-you-might-enjoy-reading-it/3/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121017110318/http://www.collapseboard.com/features/interviews/an-ancient-interview-with-yeah-yeah-yeahs-thought-you-might-enjoy-reading-it/3/ |archive-date=October 17, 2012 |access-date=March 7, 2026 |website=Collapse Board}}</ref> emphasized by the repeated lyric "As a fuck, son, you sucked!"<ref name=":1" /> The band co-wrote "Mystery Girl" with Jack Martin, which is about a sexually-promiscuous woman and her adventures.<ref name="RS" /><ref name="Pitchfork" /> "[[Art Star]]", whose lyrics satirizes [[Jet set|jet-set culture]] and the [[art world]], is the only Yeah Yeah Yeahs song with a [[spoken word]] introduction and [[Screaming in music|screaming]] vocals.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |last=Gray |first=Julia |date=June 1, 2018 |title=The 10 best Yeah Yeah Yeahs songs |url=https://stereogum.com/1999279/the-10-best-yeah-yeah-yeahs-songs/lists |access-date=March 7, 2026 |website=[[Stereogum]]}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite web |last=Frere-Jones |first=Sasha |author-link=Sasha Frere-Jones |date=February 6, 2006 |title=Positive attitude |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2006/02/13/positive-attitude |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230401151503/https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2006/02/13/positive-attitude |archive-date=April 1, 2023 |access-date=March 26, 2026 |website=[[The New Yorker]]}}</ref> "Miles Away" is about a woman that has "hurt fewer people in a better world".<ref name=":12" /> The closing track, "Our Time", is an [[anthem]] about a romance that nearly failed and perseverance,<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":8" /> which came to inspire New Yorkers after the [[September 11 attacks]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name="RSAG" />

At [[Metacritic]], which assigns a [[Standard score|normalized]] rating out of 100 to reviews from mainstream publications, ''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' received an [[Weighted arithmetic mean|average]] score of 73, indicating "generally favorable reviews".<ref name="MC" /> Critics generally praised the EP's sound; [[AllMusic]] described it as one of the most innovative releases of the 2000s [[Garage rock|garage rock revival]] at the time,<ref name="AllMusic" /> while [[Everett True]] wrote that it captured the spirit of rock n' roll.<ref name=":9" /> Karen O's performances were highlighted for additional praise, with writers for [[Blender (magazine)|''Blender'']] and ''[[CMJ]]'' describing her as "hot and sexy".<ref name=":11">{{cite magazine |last=Santangelo |first=Antonia |date=July 8, 2002 |title=Reviews |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aBw3t2fY64UC&pg=PA10-IA2 |magazine=CMJ New Music Report |page=12 |volume=72 |issue=770 |issn=0890-0795}}</ref><ref name="Blender" /> Some criticism was directed at its [[sound quality]], which was seen as limiting its potential,<ref name="RS" /> while a [[Stylus Magazine|''Stylus'']] writer found three of its five tracks unremarkable.<ref name="Stylus" /> [[Pitchfork (website)|''Pitchfork'']] noted early skepticism surrounding the rock movement but concluded that the EP demonstrated a "sharp survey" of the band's capabilities.<ref name="Pitchfork" />   

In 2002, ''[[NME]]'' ranked ''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' second on its list of the year's best singles.<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 10, 2016 |title=NME's best albums and tracks of 2002 |url=https://www.nme.com/features/2002-2-1045353 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250124234412/https://www.nme.com/features/2002-2-1045353 |archive-date=January 24, 2025 |access-date=February 12, 2026 |website=[[NME]]}}</ref> In the 2004 edition of ''[[The Rolling Stone Album Guide]]'', [[Sasha Frere-Jones]] awarded the EP four stars, writing that the band "instantly made their case for good-old-fashioned attitude"; the EP scored higher than their acclaimed debut album, ''[[Fever to Tell]]''.<ref name="RSAG" /> In 2016, ''[[Under the Radar (magazine)|Under the Radar]]'' ranked it among the best albums of its year, and said that it was essential both to the band's success and the contemporary [[Music of New York City|New York music scene]].<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Berlyant |first=Matthew |date=December 29, 2016 |title=The 15th anniversary: Yeah Yeah Yeahs' "Yeah Yeah Yeahs" EP |url=https://www.undertheradarmag.com/news/the_15th_anniversary_yeah_yeah_yeahs_yeah_yeah_yeahs_ep/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240221192539/https://www.undertheradarmag.com/news/the_15th_anniversary_yeah_yeah_yeahs_yeah_yeah_yeahs_ep/ |archive-date=February 21, 2024 |access-date=March 24, 2026 |magazine=[[Under the Radar (magazine)|Under the Radar]]}}</ref> In 2024, writers for ''[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]'' ranked it at number 42 on their list of the "100 Greatest EPs of All Time", writing that it built on the early works of contemporaries like [[the Strokes]] and [[Interpol (band)|Interpol]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=September 25, 2024 |title=The 100 Greatest EPs of All Time |url=https://www.pastemagazine.com/music/greatest-albums/the-100-greatest-eps-of-all-time |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260130195229/https://www.pastemagazine.com/music/greatest-albums/the-100-greatest-eps-of-all-time |archive-date=January 30, 2026 |access-date=March 6, 2026 |website=[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]}}</ref>

'''''Yeah Yeah Yeahs''''' (often mistitled as '''''Master''''') is the debut [[extended play]] (EP) by the American indie rock band [[Yeah Yeah Yeahs]]. After forming in 2000 and building a reputation with their live shows, Yeah Yeah Yeahs recorded and produced the EP with Jerry Teel, a member of [[Boss Hog]]. It is a record featuring the band's early [[garage rock]] and [[art punk]] influences. It was [[self-released]] on July 9, 2001, and reissued in 2002 by [[Touch and Go Records|Touch and Go]] and other [[Independent record label|independent labels]] worldwide.  

''Yeah Yeah Yeahs'' was received positively by critics and ranked by ''[[NME]]'' as the second best single of 2002. It received little attention upon release but became a [[sleeper hit]] after its reissue, topping the [[UK Independent Singles and Albums Charts|UK Indie Chart]] and exceeding sales of 71,000 units in the United States by the end of the decade. In 2024, [[Paste (magazine)|''Paste'']] ranked it among the greatest EPs ever made. 

== Background and recording ==
The singer/songwriter [[Karen O]] and guitarist [[Nick Zinner]] founded the acoustic duo Unitard in 2000. They changed their name that year to Yeah Yeah Yeahs and shifted to a "trashy, punky, [and] grimy" sound inspired by the contemporary Ohio music scene.<ref name=":02">{{Cite web |last=Houghton |first=Cillea |date=April 4, 2023 |title=Behind the New York City-inspired band name: Yeah Yeah Yeahs |url=https://americansongwriter.com/behind-the-new-york-city-inspired-band-name-yeah-yeah-yeahs/
